title: The ladder of love
hookLine: Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from one beautiful person to beauty itself (Symposium 210–211)

cards: A dinner party in Athens, in Plato's Symposium. The guests agree to go easy on the wine and take turns giving speeches in praise of love.

When it's Socrates' turn, the well-known talker does something odd: he doesn't offer his own view. A wise woman from Mantinea named Diotima taught him what love is, he says, and he simply passes her lesson on.
It has a shape, and the shape is a climb.

teach.b: First, one beautiful person. The Greek word all night is eros, love as longing, love that wants what it doesn't yet have.
Diotima says this love often begins with one beautiful person, and the lover is moved to speak beautiful words.
Second, beauty in others. The lover notices that the beauty in one body is akin to the beauty in another, and the love widens past a single face.
Third, beauty of soul: the beauty of minds and character, then of good laws and ways of living, then of knowledge.

Fourth, beauty itself. At the top, Diotima says, the lover suddenly sees a beauty that doesn't grow or fade, isn't lovely in one way and ugly in another, and is the source of every beautiful thing below it.
Readers call it the ladder of love, because she describes going up as if by steps. Some hear it as climbing away from people.
Others hear the first love as the bottom rung: not thrown away, and without it there's no ladder at all. Plato leaves room for both readings.
What's plain in the text is the direction: love, for Diotima, keeps reaching past the thing it started with.

how: Readers of Plato's Symposium, in philosophy classes and in some mystical writing shaped by Plato, discuss Diotima's ascent from the love of one person to the love of beauty itself.

o: love as longing for what you don't yet have
a love that asks for nothing and wants nothing back
a duty of kindness owed to every neighbor

games.q: who's who at the dinner — tap the pairs.
p: beauty that doesn't grow or fade
passes on what he was taught

s: at the Symposium, Socrates gives his own theory of love
he says Diotima taught him, and he passes on her lesson.
Diotima's top step is a beauty that doesn't grow or fade
and it's the source of every beautiful thing below it.
every reader agrees the ladder means leaving people behind
some hear it that way; others hear the first love as the rung the ladder stands on.

games.q: you're Socrates at the dinner party, and it's your turn to praise love. what do you do?
o: give the cleverest speech of the night.
say a wise woman taught you, and pass on her lesson.
games.why: he credits Diotima of Mantinea and repeats what she taught him: love as a climb toward beauty itself.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something beautiful near you, or bring one to mind: a face, a line of music, a kind act you once saw, an idea that made you sit up.

After a few breaths, let your attention climb one step and ask what it is in this that lifts you, not the thing itself but its beauty. If nothing comes, stay on the first rung; it's part of the ladder too.

wordCard.voice: Eros. Love as longing, the force in Plato's Symposium that climbs, step by step, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love as longing, the love the Symposium's speeches praise; Diotima's ladder is a climb of this love.

carryVoice: Your line: the ladder. The first rung counts too, and so does the climb. See you tomorrow.
